title: Introduction
content:
leaflet-geosearch adds support for geocoding (address lookup, a.k.a. geosearching) to your (web) application. It comes with controls to be embedded in your Leaflet map.

It comes with providers for OpenStreetMap, Google, Bing, Esri, LocationIQ, OpenCage and more, see the Providers section. You can also write your own.

Although this project is named leaflet-geosearch, the providers also work without Leaflet, for example to look up addresses in a form. Import them from leaflet-geosearch/providers when Leaflet isn't available, like during server-side rendering (see Usage).

Installation

Include the CSS file somewhere. Where you do this depends a bit on your build pipeline.

import 'node_modules/leaflet-geosearch/dist/geosearch.css';

Using a CDN

To load leaflet-geosearch from a CDN instead of using a bundler, use jsDelivr or unpkg. Both serve the files from the npm package:

File	Use
dist/geosearch.css	The styles of the control.
dist/bundle.min.js	For a <script> tag. Sets window.GeoSearch. dist/geosearch.umd.js is the same file.
dist/geosearch.module.js	An ES module for <script type="module">. It imports leaflet, see ES modules.

Pin the major version, like @5 below, instead of @latest. A new major version can have breaking changes, and with @latest your page would get it without notice.

Include the CSS file in the head section of your page, and the JavaScript file before the closing body tag. When you use it with Leaflet, include it after Leaflet's JavaScript file:

<link
  rel="stylesheet"
  href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/leaflet-geosearch@5/dist/geosearch.css"
/>

<!-- Make sure you put this AFTER leaflet.js, when using with leaflet -->
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/leaflet-geosearch@5/dist/bundle.min.js"></script>

<link
  rel="stylesheet"
  href="https://unpkg.com/leaflet-geosearch@5/dist/geosearch.css"
/>

<!-- Make sure you put this AFTER leaflet.js, when using with leaflet -->
<script src="https://unpkg.com/leaflet-geosearch@5/dist/bundle.min.js"></script>

For Leaflet 2, load its leaflet-global.js first, see Leaflet 2.

Now you're ready to use the control or providers. Just remember that your "import" syntax will be a bit different from what the docs are using.

// when the docs use an import:

const provider = new OpenStreetMapProvider();

// you want to get it of the window global
const provider = new GeoSearch.OpenStreetMapProvider();

ES modules

dist/geosearch.module.js imports leaflet by name, which a browser can't resolve on its own. Add an import map that points leaflet to the same Leaflet your map uses. This works well with Leaflet 2, which is published as ES modules:

<link
  rel="stylesheet"
  href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/leaflet@2.0.0-alpha.1/dist/leaflet.css"
/>
<link
  rel="stylesheet"
  href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/leaflet-geosearch@5/dist/geosearch.css"
/>

<script type="importmap">
  {
    "imports": {
      "leaflet": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/leaflet@2.0.0-alpha.1/dist/leaflet.js",
      "leaflet-geosearch": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/leaflet-geosearch@5/dist/geosearch.module.js"
    }
  }
</script>

<script type="module">
  
  

  const map = new Map('map').setView([52.09, 5.12], 8);
  new TileLayer('https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png').addTo(map);

  map.addControl(
    new GeoSearchControl({ provider: new OpenStreetMapProvider() }),
  );
</script>

Services that rewrite the imports for you, like jsDelivr's /+esm or esm.sh, load their own copy of Leaflet (leaflet@latest, which is 1.9). If your map uses a different Leaflet, the page ends up with two copies of Leaflet, and the control may not work with your map. The import map avoids that. With esm.sh, you can add ?external=leaflet so it uses the Leaflet from your import map:

"leaflet-geosearch": "https://esm.sh/leaflet-geosearch@5?external=leaflet"

Example

A basic working example would look like:

// Either get GeoSearch from the window global, or import from `leaflet-geosearch`
// 

const map = L.map('map').setView([51.505, -0.09], 13);

L.tileLayer('//tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png').addTo(map);

const search = new GeoSearch.GeoSearchControl({
  provider: new GeoSearch.OpenStreetMapProvider(),
});

map.addControl(search);

Providers

leaflet-geosearch uses so-called "providers" to take care of building the correct service URL and parsing the retrieved data into a uniform format. Thanks to this architecture, it is trivial to add your own providers, so you can use your own geocoding service.

When OpenStreetMap does not match your needs; you can also choose to use the Bing, Esri, Google, LocationIQ, or OpenCage providers. Most of those providers do however require API keys. See the documentation pages on the relevant organisations on how to obtain these keys.

In case you decide to write your own provider, please consider submitting a PR to share your work with us.

Providers are unaware of any options you can give them. They are simple proxies to their endpoints. There is only one special property, and that is the params option. The difference being; that params will be included in the endpoint url. Being Often used for API KEYS, while the other attributes can be used for provider configuration.

Browser support / Polyfills

This project is written with the latest technologies in mind. Thereby it is required to include some polyfills when you wish to support older browsers. These polyfills are recommended for IE and Safari support:

babel-polyfill, for array.includes support.

unfetch, for fetch requests.

title: Leaflet Control
description: To show the search control on your leaflet map, add the SearchControl to the leaflet map

title: AMap Provider
description: note: AMap services require an API key. Obtain here. For more options and configurations, see the AMap developer docs.

title: Bing Provider
description: note: Bing services require an API key. Obtain here. For more options and configurations, see the Microsoft developer docs.

title: Custom Providers
description: It's possible to create your own providers either by creating one from scratch, or extending an existing one. The most trivial one to extend, is the OpenStreetMap provider. As Nominatim is open source, and can be self hosted, the provider allows for easy extension. When the constructor is the only thing you need to override, it might be sufficient to provide the options during initialization: However, custom providers can be easier to share, and have a single source of truth. As you don't need to manage the URL's on various places throughout your codebase.

title: Esri Provider
description: For more options and configurations, see the ArcGIS developer docs. The provider asks for up to 5 locations. Pass maxLocations in params to change that:

title: GeoApiFr Provider
description: For more options and configurations, see the Geo Api FR.

title: Geoapify Provider
description: note: Geoapify services require an API key. Obtain geoapify. For more options and configurations, see the Geoapify developer docs.

title: Geocode Earth Provider
description: Geocode Earth is a hosted version of Pelias run by the core maintainers of the FOSS project. note: Geocode Earth services require an API key, grab a free trial key from their website. For more options and configurations, see the documentation.

title: Google Provider
description: <u>note</u>: Google services require an API key enabled for both the Geocoding API and the Maps JavaScript API (more on key configuration below). Obtain here. For more options and configurations, see the Google Maps developer docs.

title: Here Provider
description: note: Here services require an API key. Obtain here. For more options and configurations, see the Here developer docs.

title: Legacy Google Provider
description: <u>WARNING</u>: This provider is unsafe to use and should be considered <u>DEPRECATED</u>. It is strongly suggested to use the new Google Provider. If you're currently migrating from a previous version and you still wish to use this provider you should pull in the LegacyGoogleProvider class and rename your references accordingly. note: Google services require an API key. Obtain here. For more options and configurations, see the Google Maps developer docs.

title: LocationIQ Provider
description: note: LocationIQ services require an API key. Obtain here. For more options and configurations, see the LocationIQ developer docs.

title: MapBox Provider
description: note: MapBox services require an API key. Obtain here. For more options and configurations, see the MapBox developer docs on the Search API.

title: OpenCage Provider
description: note: OpenCage services require an API key. Obtain here. For more options and configurations, see the OpenCage developer docs.

title: OpenGeocoding Provider
description: note: OpenGeocoding requires an API key. Create one in the dashboard. For use in a web page, create a browser key and restrict it to your site's origins. The key is sent in a header, never in the url. Suggestions while typing come from the autocomplete endpoint and don't count as requests. They have no coordinates, so picking one looks it up by its id, and that counts as one request. Reverse geocoding counts as one request too. See the API docs.

title: OpenStreetMap Provider

toc.text: Limiting the results to an area

description: For more options and configurations, see the OpenStreetMap Nominatim wiki.

title: PdokNl Provider
description: For more options and configurations, see the PDOK Locatieserver.

title: Pelias Provider
description: Pelias is an open-source geocoder powered completely by open data, available freely to everyone. In order to use this provider you'll need to have your own Pelias server running. The Docker repository provides the quickest path to running your own server. See the Pelias documentation for more detailed information about the available endpoints and query parameters. Looking for a hosted version of Pelias? check out the Geocode Earth provider.

title: Photon Provider
description: Photon is an open-source geocoder for OpenStreetMap data, built for search as you type. It works without an API key. The public server at photon.komoot.io is free for reasonable use, without guarantees. For heavy traffic, run your own server and point the provider to it with host.

title: Upgrading
content:
Each major version has its own upgrade notes: what changed, and how to get the old behaviour back where that's possible.

toc.text: A picked suggestion isn't searched again

description: 5.0 fixes a lot of long-standing issues, and some of those fixes change what you see. The API is the same: nothing was removed or renamed, and the browser support didn't change. Each section shows what changed from 4.x (red) to 5.0 (green), and how to get the old behaviour back if you relied on it.

title: Usage
description: There are two ways in which leaflet-geosearch can be used. Direct usage, for example for address forms, or embedded in a leaflet map to search for points of interest.
